2) Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) — Common red, friable vascular nodule that can arise on the ear; typically bleeds easily and can grow rapidly, but a variant can be less symptomatic.  
3) Cutaneous hemangioma / vascular malformation — A benign vascular lesion can present as a soft, reddish superficial nodule and would explain color and softness.  
4) Epidermal inclusion cyst (sebaceous/epidermoid cyst) — Possible as a superficial, mobile nodule; less consistent with red color but can become erythematous if inflamed.  
5) Keloid / hypertrophic scar — Less likely given no history of trauma/piercing and the soft consistency, but earlobe is a common site and raised scar tissue can appear reddish.

Recommended next steps to confirm diagnosis and guide management (strongly advised):
- Excisional biopsy of the lesion with histopathologic examination (definitive diagnosis).  
- If excision not immediately feasible, perform high-frequency ultrasound or Doppler of the lesion to assess vascularity (helps distinguish vascular tumors vs cystic/solid lesions).  
- CBC with differential (check for eosinophilia which may support ALHE).  
- Dermatology or ENT referral for procedural planning if lesion is vascular or cosmetically sensitive.
